intro: In this college you'll learn the Dutch for household appliances, gas, water and electricity, how to save money on your energy bill, how to give and get advice, and how to arrange for a repairman to come by when something is broken.

paragraphs.heading: Welcome — the house you live in
paragraphs.text: Welcome to theme thirteen. Its title is a friendly one: [[We gebruiken het iedere dag]], which means 'we use it every day'. And it is true — every single day you use machines and energy in your home, usually without thinking about them. The general word for a household machine or device is [[het apparaat]], and the plural is [[de apparaten]]. Let's name the big ones. The washing machine is [[de wasmachine]]. The fridge is [[de koelkast]]. The dishwasher is [[de afwasmachine]]. And the heating is [[de verwarming]]. These four words come back constantly, so say them out loud with me now. There is a warm Dutch saying that fits this whole theme: [[Oost west, thuis best]], which literally means 'east, west, home is best' — in other words, there is no place like home. In this college I explain everything in English, but every Dutch word and sentence is spoken by a native voice, so your ear gets used to the real sounds. Try to repeat each phrase after me. By the end you will be able to say what is broken, ask someone to fix it, and even pick up a money-saving tip or two. Ready? [[Laten we beginnen!]]

paragraphs.heading: Gas, water and electricity
paragraphs.text: Dutch homes run on three things you pay for, and you must know their names. Gas is [[het gas]]; many people cook and heat with it. Water is [[het water]]. And electricity, or power, is [[de stroom]] — you will also hear the longer word [[elektriciteit]]. The bill that arrives for all of this is [[de rekening]], and the specific energy bill is [[de energierekening]]. Energy is not cheap in the Netherlands, so people watch this bill carefully. A very common, honest sentence is [[De rekening voor gas en licht is hoog]], which means 'the bill for gas and electricity is high'. Notice the word [[licht]] there — it literally means 'light', but Dutch people often say it to mean electricity in the home. This theme also teaches the little word [[zonder]], which means 'without', and it is always followed straight by a noun: [[zonder gas]], [[zonder water]], [[zonder stroom]]. You can build a strong sentence with it: [[We kunnen niet zonder elektriciteit]], 'we can't do without electricity'. Or, more relaxed: [[Hij kan prima zonder televisie]], 'he can manage just fine without a TV'. So [[zonder]] plus a noun is your easy formula for saying what you can or cannot live without.

paragraphs.heading: When something is broken: kapot
paragraphs.text: Now the most important word of the whole theme: [[kapot]], which means 'broken'. You will need it the day a machine stops working — and that day always comes. The basic pattern is the thing, plus [[is]], plus [[kapot]]. So: [[De wasmachine is kapot]], 'the washing machine is broken'. Or [[De koelkast is kapot]], 'the fridge is broken'. There is a softer, very Dutch way to say the same thing: [[Het apparaat doet het niet meer]], which means 'the appliance doesn't work anymore'. Listen to that phrase [[doet het niet meer]] — Dutch people use it all the time for machines that have given up. You might also point at the plug, which is [[de stekker]], and check it is in the socket. Here a small grammar point helps: the word [[als]] means 'if' or 'when', and it lets you describe the problem. For example: [[Als ik hem aanzet, gebeurt er niets]], 'when I switch it on, nothing happens'. Notice that after the comma the verb comes first: [[gebeurt er niets]]. That is the famous Dutch rule — when a sentence starts with [[Als]], the second part begins with the verb. Try it: [[Als de wasmachine kapot is, bel ik de monteur.]]

paragraphs.heading: Modal verbs: must, can, want
paragraphs.text: To arrange anything, you need three little helper verbs called modal verbs, and this theme reviews them. The first is [[moeten]], which means 'must' or 'have to'. For example: [[Ik moet de rekening vandaag betalen]], 'I have to pay the bill today'. The second is [[kunnen]], 'can' or 'to be able to': [[Kun je de afwasmachine repareren?]], 'can you repair the dishwasher?'. The third is [[willen]], 'to want': [[We willen een nieuw apparaat kopen]], 'we want to buy a new appliance'. Here is the golden rule that makes these easy. The modal verb comes second in the sentence and is conjugated, and the main verb jumps to the very end as an infinitive. So you say [[Ik wil de monteur bellen]], 'I want to call the repairman', with [[bellen]] right at the end — never [[Ik wil bel]]. Let's hear that pattern again with each verb: [[Ik moet de verwarming aanzetten]], [[Ik kan het niet maken]], [[Ik wil hulp vragen]]. The repairman himself is [[de monteur]], the repair is [[de reparatie]], and if you rent your home, your landlord is [[de verhuurder]] — often the person you must call first. Practise these verbs, because they unlock polite requests.

paragraphs.heading: Giving and getting tips to save energy
paragraphs.text: Because energy costs so much, Dutch people love sharing money-saving tips, and you should join in. The key verb is [[besparen]], 'to save'. The big question is [[Hoe kan ik energie besparen?]], 'how can I save energy?'. The classic answer uses an [[als]]-sentence again: [[Zet het licht uit als je weggaat]], 'switch off the light when you leave'. Another good one: [[Als je het licht uitzet, bespaar je stroom]], 'if you switch off the light, you save power'. When someone gives you helpful advice, the warm thing to say is [[Dat is een goede tip!]], 'that's a good tip!'. You can ask a neighbour directly: [[Heb jij misschien een goede tip om energie te besparen?]] To show you already do your bit, you might add [[Ik gebruik de afwasmachine iedere dag]], using the theme's title phrase [[iedere dag]], 'every day'. There is a lovely Dutch proverb for being careful with small things: [[Wie het kleine niet eert, is het grote niet waard]] — roughly, 'who does not value the small is not worthy of the large'. In practice, turning off one light, taking a shorter shower, or running [[de wasmachine]] only when full really does lower [[de energierekening]]. Small habits, real savings.

paragraphs.heading: Calling the repair service — and well done!
paragraphs.text: Let's put it all together with a real phone call. Your washing machine has died, so you ring a repair service. They answer: [[Goedemiddag, met Reparatieservice De Vries]]. You explain: [[Mijn wasmachine is kapot. Hij doet het niet meer.]] They ask what is wrong: [[Wat is er precies aan de hand?]], 'what exactly is the matter?'. You describe it: [[Als ik hem aanzet, gebeurt er niets.]] Then comes the key sentence of the whole theme, the one you must memorise: [[Wanneer kunt u langskomen?]], which means 'when can you come by?'. The verb [[langskomen]] means 'to come by', and it is exactly what you want the monteur to do. You can also ask politely [[Kunt u langskomen om het te repareren?]], 'can you come by to repair it?'. Two more money questions: [[Hoeveel kost het om het te maken?]], 'how much does it cost to fix it?', and you may hear that the call-out charge, [[het voorrijden]], costs fifty euros. You agree warmly: [[Prima. Tot morgen om tien uur, bedankt!]] And when it is all fixed, you can smile and say [[Het is weer pico bello in orde]], 'it's in perfect order again'. You have done so well today. [[Heel goed gedaan!]] See you in the next theme!
